title: Discussion and Conflict
paragraphs: As on every other day, Javid Bey and his team had gathered in the meeting room to discuss the state of the project they were working on. Each in turn gave a brief account of the successes of the previous day and of the difficulties they had met.

Then it was Kamal's turn. Like the others he reported on the work he had done, but he spoke at greater length about the problem he faced, as though hoping for help from his colleagues. The moment he finished, Nadir, in an accusing tone, stung Kamal before everyone's eyes: «You yourself are to blame; because of you our work has stopped as well, and we can do nothing.» Those in the room froze. Kamal was deeply embarrassed and did not know what to do.

As project leader, Javid Bey intervened at once so that the exchange would not swell into a conflict, and addressed the team: «Children, if you like, let us end the discussion for today, and we will settle this matter at another time.» Everyone dispersed.

Javid Bey knew well what to do: to meet one to one and talk as friends. On the pretext of a glass of tea he invited Nadir to the company café; after some talk of this and that he at last came to the point and said, calmly and without losing his composure: «My boy, your conduct toward Kamal today was very wrong. To accuse someone without learning the truth of the matter — and before others, at that — is unacceptable. Put yourself in his place. A man who looks to us for help is instead accused. I am sure Kamal hoped that we would sit together, think, and find a solution as one.»
Nadir lowered his head in shame. Javid Bey's counsel had borne fruit and become a good lesson for Nadir; he understood that he had done wrong.

Later, whenever the occasion arose, he would recall that conversation between them and say how grateful he remained to Javid Bey. One important point was this: no one else in the company ever learned of that talk.
Conflict seeks who is right; discussion seeks what is right. If you wish to find the truth, do not quarrel — discuss.

title: Compassion
paragraphs: It was a cold winter night. I was returning home from work. Ahead I saw a man who looked as if he were drunk. Swaying from side to side, utterly spent, he clung to a post beside him. I drew near. He must have been a little past thirty. He was dressed very cleanly and neatly. Some of the passers-by spoke aloud of the harm of drink; others mocked and laughed.
— Are you all right? Do you need anything? — I asked the man.
In a sound like a moan from his lips:
— I am ill!.. — he said.

So that he would not fall I took him by the waist with my arm and brought him to the taxi stand. We began to wait for a taxi. The snow that had stopped in the evening began to fall again; on the slowly icing roads no sign of life remained but the stray dogs racing one another.
I had nearly given up hope of finding a taxi when one stopped beside us. I explained the situation to the driver and said that we were in a hurry.
We seated the sick man in the back and set off for the hospital. Bless the doctors — they did at once everything that was needed and gave him medicine; we waited at the head of his bed.

The doctor on duty told us that we had at least saved the patient from freezing. The young man still could not speak, so he only looked at us and smiled. The driver was beside me too... After a while our patient came to himself. We put him in the car again and took him home.

His wife, knowing that he often fell into a diabetic coma, had come out into the street in terrible anxiety with their son. Seeing us they ran to us in excitement. The family members held one another tight, their eyes full of joy.
Of the weariness of those long hours not a trace remained; our own eyes filled at the happiness of that family, which did not know how to thank us.
At parting I asked the driver what I owed him.
He shook his head:

— You owe me nothing; on the contrary, I owe you, my friend! — he said. — You made me a partner in such a kindness. For letting a man who may for twenty years have forgotten what it is to weep live through this beautiful feeling — I am in your debt.
As I embraced the driver and we parted I did not feel the cold of the night, and I decided to walk home.
Who knows? Perhaps along the way another person would appear who needed my help?
Humanity is built upon compassion. Compassion is not to weep with the one who weeps, but to find the way to stop the tears.

title: Mockery Is Unacceptable
paragraphs: From their earliest years we must teach our children that it is unacceptable to mock others for their difference or their outward appearance and so to demean them.
To ridicule another's difference or looks is baseness. We must teach this to our children from the earliest age.

title: Why People Shout When They Argue
paragraphs: One day during a lesson the teacher put a question to his students:
— Why do people shout when they argue?
— Because they cannot rein in their nerves, — answered one student.
— But the person you are arguing with is right beside you; what need is there to shout? Can you not speak with him calmly? If you are angry, why must you shout? — the teacher deepened his question.
Each of the students offered an answer, yet none satisfied the teacher. At last he said:

— The more people grow dissatisfied with one another and argue, the farther their hearts draw apart. From that distance they must shout in order to hear each other. The louder they shout, the farther apart their hearts must be.
After a short silence the teacher went on:

— And what happens when people love one another? They do not shout; on the contrary, they speak softly. For their hearts are very near, and the distance between them is small. And what happens when love is still stronger? Then they do not even speak softly — they whisper, and draw a little closer still. As their hearts draw near they no longer even need to whisper — they simply look at one another and understand everything without words... Dear students, when you argue, do not let your hearts draw apart; do not say words that could widen the distance between you.
For one day that distance may grow so great that you will not find the way back.
A shout is the sound of hearts drawing apart. In love a whisper is enough — do not widen the distance between you.

title: The Sound of the Doorbell...
paragraphs: Last winter I was dismissed from my job. To make ends meet I had to work for a time as a newspaper deliveryman. At one of the houses I served the mailbox was sealed, so I had to knock at the door. An elderly man opened it.
— Uncle, why have you sealed the mailbox? — I asked.
— I sealed it on purpose, — he answered.
Then he smiled in a strange way and went on:
— I ask you, every day when you bring the paper, please knock at the door or ring the bell and hand it to me in person.
— Of course, but that is inconvenient for both of us; it is a waste of time, — I said in surprise.
— No problem; I am at home every day, — he said, and added:
— My wife has passed away, my son is abroad, and I live here alone. Who knows how much life is left to me?
Then I saw the old man's misted, moist eyes.
— Have you not subscribed in order to read the newspaper? — I asked.
— I never read the newspaper... I have subscribed only to the sound of the doorbell.
Then, clasping his hands together, he said:
— Young man, please do me a kindness! Here is my son's telephone number. If one day you knock and cannot get word of me, call my son and let him know.
For some people a doorbell's ring, a greeting, is worth the whole world. Let us not forget to knock at the doors of those who are alone.

title: People Who Need Something from You
paragraphs: Instead of taking offence at those who «seek you out only when they need something,» if you think that they may be in difficulty, may need your help, and that is why they seek you, your heart will grow much calmer.
Instead of resenting those who seek you only when they need something, think that they come because they trust you — and your heart will be at ease.

title: Your Friends
paragraphs: One day a young man decided to marry. After spending a week on wedding preparations he said to his father one evening: «Father, I have a request. I have not the strength to manage everything alone. Please take this list and telephone all my friends on it and invite them to my wedding.» «Gladly, my son!» his father answered.
On the wedding day the young man approached his father in an agitated state: «Father, I asked you to telephone all my friends!»
— Son, I did exactly as you wished.
— There were fifty names on my list, yet here I see only fifteen, — the young man voiced his unease again.

— My son, I telephoned every one of the fifty, one by one. To each I said that I was calling in your name, that you had a problem just then, that you needed your friends' help, and that I asked them to be at this place at this time. Do not worry at all, my son. Your true friends are here today, at your side!
A true friend is the one who stands beside you when you are in trouble. It is not the many acquaintances that matter, but the few friends who have stood the test.

title: To Meet and to Know
paragraphs: Of some people one can say only this:
We met — we were glad; we came to know them — we were saddened.
Acquaintance brings joy; knowing does not always please. To see a person as he truly is sometimes brings disappointment.

title: How to Ward Off Insults
paragraphs: (An instructive story drawn from the life of the samurai)

There was once an aged, wise samurai. He taught his pupils the secrets of wisdom and of the art of combat. One day during a lesson a warrior known for his insolence and cruelty entered the class. This warrior would insult his opponents and drive them out of patience, then exploit the mistakes that the angered opponent made one after another and defeat him. This time too he used the same tactic and spoke several insulting words to the samurai to provoke him to fight. Paying no heed to the insults, the samurai continued his lesson.
After repeating his insults several times and receiving no answer from the samurai, the warrior left the class in anger.
The pupils who had watched the scene attentively asked their teacher:
— Master, why did you endure these insults? Why did you not challenge him to a fight?
The wise samurai answered thus:
— If someone comes to you with a gift and you do not accept that gift, to whom does the gift belong?
— To its former owner, — the pupils answered.
— Envy, hatred, and insults must be looked at with the same eye. When you do not accept them, such «gifts» remain with those who try to address them to you.
An insult you do not accept returns to its owner — just like a gift that is given back. Answer evil not with evil, but with composure.

title: To Be Alone
paragraphs: I had gone to visit an acquaintance. I entered his house and went into his room. He sat in silence with his head bowed. He looked sorrowful.
— Are you sad? — I asked. He raised his head, looked into my eyes, and answered: — No, I am alone.
The greatest sorrow is to feel alone even among people. To see the loneliness of the one beside you is true sensitivity.

title: Spend Your Time with People
paragraphs: Because my father had to transfer money, I had to spend an hour with him at the bank. At last my patience ran out and I said to him:
— Father, let's do your bank business over the internet. What do you say?
— What will that give me, son? — my father looked at me in surprise.
— You will no longer waste an hour at the bank to transfer money. The internet will even let you do your shopping online. Everything will be so easy and convenient, — I answered quickly.
The prospect of drawing my father into the world of the internet had greatly excited me.
My father asked:
— If I do as you say, then I won't have to leave the house. Is that it?
— Exactly, exactly, Father.
I even told him that the groceries he bought could be brought to the door, that the Amazon company delivered everything to the buyer's home.
At my father's answer my tongue went dry in my mouth:
— My son, in the hour I spent at the bank I saw four of my friends and talked with the bank clerks who have known me well for a long time.
You know that I am alone... I need to see people. I like to dress and go to the bank. I have enough time, and I have always taken pleasure in living conversation.
Two years ago when I fell ill, the seller from the nearby shop where I always bought fruit came to see me; he was very distressed that I was sick, sat by my bed, and shared in my condition.
Not long ago when your mother fell during her morning walk, the grocer from our neighbourhood helped her up, put her in his car, and brought her home at once. Because he knew where we lived.
If everything were online, would I not be deprived of these human feelings?
Why, after all, should I communicate only with a computer so that everything may be brought as far as my door?
I want to know the person I deal with instead of an «electronic seller.» I want living contact, a relationship.
Can Amazon do that as well?
Technology is not life.
Spend your time with people, not with devices, my son.
Technology gives convenience, but it does not replace life. True value lies in living conversation, in the warmth between one person and another.

title: Welcome, My Bey
paragraphs: When my late father, Hafiz Ali, was at Çanakkale, I was still in my mother's womb, seven months along. I never saw my father, never knew him. There was not even a photograph of him.
They were very hard days. Mobilization, the years of occupation, liberation, poverty, hardship...
Our childhood passed in a constant chase after bread, amid suffering.
Whenever my mother wished to go somewhere she would always come to me and say:
— My son, I am going to the market. If your father comes, tell me at once!
— I am going to my sister's. If your father comes, tell me at once!
— I am going to the neighbour's. If your father comes, tell me at once!
My mother kept her eyes always on the road, waiting for my father.
I grew up, found work, opened a shop. As always, when my mother was going somewhere she would come to the shop, say where she was going, and add: «If your father comes, let me know, won't you!»
Years passed. My mother grew old. Even so she remained true to her habit and, leaning on her stick, would come to me and say: «If your father comes, call me, won't you!»
One day her condition worsened and she took to her bed.

On the threshold of death she took leave of us: «You looked after me well; forgive me any debt I owe you,» she said. Slowly she turned toward me and said: «If your father comes, tell him that your mother always waited for him.» Suddenly something happened: she raised her head, looked toward the door, and smiling said: «Welcome, my bey, welcome!» — and gave up her soul.
From the memoirs of Cevdet Algalp, an elderly cobbler living in Balıkesir.
Recorded by: researcher and writer Mustafa Doğru, geography teacher at Bursa Çınar Anadolu High School.
The eighteenth of March is the day of the victory at Çanakkale.

Had Çanakkale fallen in 1915, invented states would have been set up in Anatolia, the peoples living there would have been turned into enemies and made to slaughter one another, and the country would have become a colony of the English, the French, and the Italians.
May the souls of all the martyrs rejoice — among them our Azerbaijani soldiers who fell as martyrs at Çanakkale! May no mother's eyes remain fixed upon the road!
A mother's lifelong fidelity and waiting is the purest expression of love. Sacred is the memory of those who died for the homeland and of the mothers whose eyes stayed upon the road.

title: If the Road Does Not Tire You, It Is Because of Your Companion
paragraphs: My mother used to tell: «I married your father when I was very young. I could neither cook a proper meal nor take up a needle for embroidery and sewing. One day my mother-in-law — your grandmother — as she was getting ready to visit a neighbour, spread before me a quilt whose wool she had washed and dried and said: “You will have quilted this by the time I return.” I began to quilt, but I had not the strength. The needle would not pass through the quilt. Tears came over me. On the one hand the needle pricked my hand and my eyes watered with pain; on the other I did not know what to say to my mother-in-law, and my tears would not cease.

Just then your father came home for the midday break. Seeing me in tears he took the needle in his hand, in a short time finished quilting the quilt and set it aside. Then he ate his meal and went back to work. He said nothing to my mother-in-law. When the woman returned home she saw that the quilt was quite ready and was very pleased.»
Not for nothing do they say: «If the road does not tire you, it is because of your companion.»
It is not the road that tires you or lightens your load, but the person at your side. A true companion makes even hard work easy.

title: To Forgive
paragraphs: To forgive someone does not mean to love him; it does not mean that you are obliged to speak with him or continue the relationship; it does not mean that you accept that he was innocent or in the right.
To forgive someone means to free yourself from the prison of disappointment, resentment, and hatred — to feel no longer the pain of the wound that was dealt you.
Forgive and be free. Forgive, but never forget — or you will be wounded again.
Forgiveness is not declaring the other side right — it is freeing yourself from the prison of rancour and resentment. Forgive and find peace, but do not forget the lesson either.
